document.description: MetH/MSMEG_4185 is the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase of Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc²155. It transfers methyl groups from methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine through an enzyme-bound cobalamin intermediate, producing methionine and tetrahydrofolate. Its modular protein contains homocysteine-, folate-, cobalamin- and SAM-associated regions; zinc supports activation of homocysteine. In the native strain, endogenous cobalamin suppresses the alternative MetE route, making MetH necessary under the tested conditions. Disabling cobalamin synthesis relieves that dependence by permitting MetE use.

document.description: MetE/MSMEG_6638 is the full-length, cobalamin-independent methionine synthase of Mycolicibacterium smegmatis mc²155. Its folate- and homocysteine-binding architecture supports zinc-dependent transfer of a methyl group from methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, producing methionine. Unlike compact MesD or MesB proteins, it contains the canonical N-terminal folate-associated and C-terminal catalytic domains. Endogenous cobalamin represses its expression through a riboswitch, favoring the alternative MetH route; when cobalamin synthesis is disabled, MetE can sustain methionine biosynthesis.

document.description: Tm0936/MtaD is a zinc-dependent deaminase from Thermotoga maritima MSB8 that converts S-adenosylhomocysteine to S-inosylhomocysteine and 5′-methylthioadenosine to 5′-methylthioinosine. It also deaminates adenosine and 5′-deoxyadenosine in purified-protein assays. Its measured substrate profile favors the sulfur-containing adenosine derivatives in the 2013 comparison. Coupling SAH deamination to the organism's SIH-hydrolyzing AhcY can regenerate homocysteine, although the dominant native substrate and flux through that route remain unresolved. AMP and SAM were not substrates in the original assay.

document.description: AhcY/TM_0172 is a soluble NAD-dependent adenosylhomocysteinase from Thermotoga maritima MSB8. It reversibly hydrolyzes S-adenosylhomocysteine to adenosine and homocysteine and also hydrolyzes S-inosylhomocysteine to inosine and homocysteine. Both substrates were processed approximately equally in the direct comparative assay. The internal NAD cofactor supports the redox-assisted carbon–sulfur bond cleavage. Its SIH activity can complete the chemical sequence initiated by MtaD-mediated SAH deamination; the contribution of that sequence to native metabolic flux has not been established.

document.title: Bacterial methionine cycle and homocysteine remethylation
document.description: A bacterial cycle converts L-methionine to S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM), uses SAM in SAH-producing methyl-transfer reactions, regenerates homocysteine by alternative SAH-processing chemistries, and remethylates homocysteine. Direct SAH hydrolysis, Pfs/LuxS cleavage and deamination followed by SIH hydrolysis have distinct enzyme and evidence requirements. Homocysteine remethylation varies with folate, cobalamin, external methyl donors and enzyme partners. De novo sulfur assimilation, donor uptake, methylthioadenosine salvage and downstream AI-2 reception are adjacent biology. The cycle is an open metabolic system requiring energy and methyl input, not a claim of universal bacterial distribution or demonstrated native flux in every represented species.

document.summary: NAD-dependent S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolases cleave the product of SAM-dependent methylation to adenosine and homocysteine, relieving product inhibition of methyltransferases (bacterial AhcY, S. cerevisiae SAH1, S. pombe sah1/pi047, human AHCY, plant SAHH). Vertebrate AHCYL1 (IRBIT) and AHCYL2 are non-catalytic paralogs that regulate the IP3 receptor and ion transporters.
